I'm tracing the `ValueError` regarding a missing cached object. It seems `self.has_cached_object()` is unexpectedly returning `False`, despite the object being present in `self._cache`. I'm now examining the `__getattr__` implementation to see how the cache is being managed and updated.

**Debugging Cache Logic**

I've identified a critical flaw: accessing `self._cache` directly, if not yet initialized via `__pydantic_private__`, returns `NotSet` via `__getattr__`. This is happening even after `_cache_object` appears to set it, as `__setattr__`'s handling of underscored attributes conflicts.

# Database is locked
created: 2025-03-23, last updated: 2025-11-20, [Read more](https://www.reddit.com/r/sqlite/comments/1ji9jfi/database_is_locked/)

To achieve the expected behavior, you must configure the busy_timeout setting for each individual connection.
You can find more details on this here:://www.org/.html#pragma_timeout.
Additionally, ensure that you initiate your transactions with BEGIN IMMEDIATE instead of just BEGIN.
Using BEGIN alone will create a deferred transaction, which won't try to obtain a write lock until the first INSERT or UPDATE occurs.
...
When one program initiates a transaction that locks the database, other requests to the database will typically have to wait until the lock is released.
However, SQLite operates differently.
By default, it will check for database locks and, if it detects one, it will return a failure instead of waiting.
To address this, you can implement a `busy_timeout`, which allows the system to wait for a specified duration (up to N milliseconds) before failing.
For instance, you can set it with `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 10000`.
...
Setting your busy timeout to around 10 seconds should suffice, as each write operation generally completes in under one second.
...
On a brighter note, I was able to test `PRAGMA busy_timeout=10000`, and it seems to be effective.

I’ve recently discovered that SQLite can raise a `database is locked` error without trying to retry to acquire a lock, making the `timeout` setting irrelevant.
...
Trying to acquire a lock in the middle of an active transaction can make SQLite throw the db is locked error immediately instead of retrying until the timeout is up.
The solution (I think) is to force SQLite to open the transaction in immediate mode instead of deferred (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` instead of `BEGIN`), but the proposal to do this was rejected 5 years ago.
...
At this point I think the only acceptable solution, assuming this gets some traction (this issue has seen no activity for over 5 years) would be to allow specifying whether or not all transaction start should be immediate though an `OPTIONS` which is what I assume Aymeric was alluding to
```
...
DATABASES = {
"default": {
"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3",
"OPTIONS": {
# The following two options alleviate sqlite "database is locked" errors
# See https://forum.djangoproject.com/t/sqlite-and-database-is-locked-error/26994
"transaction_mode": "IMMEDIATE",
"timeout": 20,
},
},
}
